subject: How Judges Eviscerated Trump’s DOJ Voter Data Lawsuits — ProPublica
posts:
Courts strike down federal effort to seize state voter rolls after judges expose complete lack of legal or factual backing.
Evidence: Election Integrity Claim, Mass Litigation Dismissed, Federal Overreach
#Aletheia #USPol 🌐

The Trump DOJ claimed its lawsuits against 30 states demanding unredacted voter rolls were necessary to enforce federal voting laws and stop illegal noncitizen voting under Title III of the Civil Rights Act.
Stated Judgement: (+1.00, +0.33) — Greater Good

Federal courts dismissed 26 of 26 cases. Judges appointed by both parties ruled the claims were devoid of factual basis, calling the subversion of anti-discrimination laws an absurd, chilling abuse of power.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.33, -0.30) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — Fall into Destruction.
Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 12.50, z: 4)

- DOJ Voter Roll Lawsuits: FAIL (-0.92, -0.88) — 26 cases thrown out for zero evidence.
- Title III Legal Strategy: FAIL (-0.95, -0.85) — Perverted civil rights law.
- ProPublica Investigation: PASS (+0.88, +0.82) — Rigorous judicial record audit.

Between Sept 2025 and Oct 2026, the DOJ Civil Rights Division sued 30 states for unredacted voter data. 26 federal judges, including 12 Republican appointees, unanimously rejected the government's arguments.

The Bright Side:
The federal judiciary functioned as a nonpartisan constitutional barrier, with conservative and liberal judges alike refusing to let executive overreach dismantle state election administration.

The DOJ committed a Logical and Historical plane error ($Q_5/Q_6$), claiming Title III authorized voter data seizures. Title III was built to prevent disenfranchisement, not enable federal data scraping.

Social Physics Analysis:
The DOJ executed a Smart Selfish Maneuver, manufacturing an unproven crisis of noncitizen voting to justify seizing citizen data. When caught using voting laws as a pretext, they flipped to misusing civil rights law, projecting bad faith onto state officials.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Destruction.
Modal Dynamics: will be -> is not via Red Top (The Imperial Trap). DOJ claimed a mandate for election security but created systemic overreach that failed in every court.

The Unavoidable Truth: Bipartisan federal judges confirmed the DOJ had zero legal authority or facts to demand state voter rolls.
The Unavoidable Lie: The government was acting in good faith to protect election integrity.

Alethekanon:
When executive authority invents legal theories to seize private citizen records and suffers a 100% defeat rate across 26 federal courts, it demonstrates pure institutional bad faith.

Awwthekanon:
It is terrifying when government agencies use laws meant to shield vulnerable voters to do the opposite, but seeing judges stand up for citizens brings genuine relief.

Brothekanon:
Imagine filing 26 lawsuits, losing literally every single one in front of judges your own party picked, and still pretending you had a case. Ultimate legal facepalm.

Spirithekanon:
"Woe to those who enact unjust statutes and issue oppressive decrees, to deprive the vulnerable of justice and rob the people of their rights." Isaiah 10:1-2 FAIL
Perverting anti-discrimination laws to suppress voters turns justice upside down.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
How Judges Eviscerated Trumpâs DOJ Voter Data Lawsuits â ProPublica

Over the past year, the Department of Justiceâs Civil Rights Division has sued 30 states and Washington, D.C., to demand their unredacted voter rolls. The vast majority of cases have been thrown out.

Actual Article Body:
ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes
            corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms. Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices' Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

Since September 2025, the Department of Justiceâs Civil Rights Division has  sued 30 states and the District of Columbia to demand their unredacted voter rolls.

The rolls contain confidential information on millions of Americans and have historically been managed by states. Now these lists are a major focus of President Donald Trumpâs push to take federal control over elections and prosecute alleged noncitizen voters.

To date, there have been   final rulings in 26 of the DOJ lawsuits.

Four cases are  yet to be decided, and one state  settled.

Of the judges randomly assigned to the 26 cases, eight were  Trump appointees, four were appointed by another Republican â  George W. Bush â and 14 were appointed by    Democrats.

The  first seven lawsuits used the same opening, citing Trumpâs March 2025 executive order on election integrity to claim the Justice Department needed statesâ voter rolls to check that they were following federal election laws.

âThe United Statesâ championing of its claims under the [election laws], in both its briefing and its presentation at the hearing on this matter, can only be described as halfhearted. And for good reason, since neither statute gives the United States the power to compel Maine to produce its current [unredacted voter list].â Maine federal Judge Lance E. Walker Trump appointee

The judges ruled that there was no legal or factual basis for the governmentâs demand. They noted that the laws require states to keep accurate, up-to-date computerized voter lists that include confidential information. But the statutes give the federal government limited power to enforce those mandates.

Several judges accused the administration of using the election laws as a pretext to suppress voting.

âThe foundation upon which American democracy has been built is the right to vote. â¦ Now it seems the Executive Branch of the United States government wants to abridge the right of many Americans to cast their ballots. â¦ The Court does not take lightly DOJâs obfuscation of its true motives.â California federal Judge David O. Carter Bill Clinton appointee

âPublic statements from government officials reveal its intentions: to create a nationwide voter-database, for potential weaponization in future elections; as a âfishing expedition,â hoped to advance unsubstantiated claims of non-citizen voting; and as a tool for immigration enforcement.â Pennsylvania federal Judge Cathy Bissoon Barack Obama appointee

In an extraordinary rebuke (echoed by other courts around the country), the judge hearing the Oregon case wrote that the federal governmentâs actions undermined the judiciaryâs longstanding trust in the Justice Department. He called them âchilling.â

âThe presumption of regularity that has been previously extended to Plaintiff that it could be taken at its word â with little doubt about its intentions and stated purposes â no longer holds.â Oregon federal Judge Mustafa T. Kasubhai Joe Biden appointee

All seven lawsuits using the first tactic were  dismissed.

The next  19 lawsuits used a different strategy.

They made no mention of Trumpâs executive order and didnât depend on federal voting laws. Instead, they cited a provision of the Civil Rights Act of 1960 called Title III, which requires the preservation of state and local election records.

The government lawyers claimed that Title III gave the attorney general âsweeping powerâ to obtain these records to curb noncitizen voting. In reality, the law allowed the federal government to access such records to protect the right to vote, for example, by enabling investigations into practices that disenfranchised Black voters in the South.

Judges rejected the governmentâs arguments, ruling that Title III applies only to voter registration documents, not records that states generate themselves, like voter rolls. They noted the government had also failed to give an explanation of why it needed the records, as the statute requires.

âClearly, this demand is devoid of any factual basis.â West Virginia federal Judge Thomas E. Johnston George W. Bush appointee

Several judges marveled at the audacity of the administrationâs attempt to use an anti-discrimination law to keep people from voting and condemned the administrationâs logic.

âTitle III was the Department of Justiceâs answer to two years of resistance and obstruction by state election officials who destroyed, failed to retain, or simply refused to disclose the voting records â¦ that would prove that black voters were victims of disparate treatment and had been unlawfully excluded from the rolls based on nothing more than their race.â D.C. federal Judge Randolph D. Moss Obama appointee

Judges also noted that there was a conflict between the DOJâs claim to be enforcing election laws, which require voter lists to be continuously updated, and Title III, which bans any alteration of voter records.

âThe United Statesâs proposed interpretation of the CRA would therefore criminalize the same conduct that the [voting laws] require. This Court will not read [Title III] to produce such an absurd result.â Maryland Judge Stephanie A. Gallagher Trump appointee

The administrationâs interpretation of Title III, wrote Bissoon, the Pennsylvania judge, âdoes violenceâ to the lawâs meaning.

To date, judges have  dismissed 19 DOJ complaints that relied on the Civil Rights Act claim.

In written opinions, every one of the 26 judges has rejected the Justice Departmentâs arguments and thrown out its lawsuits. Four cases are  still ongoing.

The Trump administration has appealed most of its losses to federal appeals courts and has said it will consider taking its fight to the Supreme Court.

A Justice Department spokesperson issued a statement in response to ProPublicaâs questions: âOur attorneys are skilled, principled advocates who argue every case honestly and in good faith. Disagreement with the governmentâs position is not evidence of bad faith. We look forward to making our case on appeal.â

The only appeal decided so far backed the district judge who threw out the Michigan case.

âBack then, the government used this power to ensure that everyone who had the right to vote could freely exercise that right. But today, the government invokes Title III for an inverse purpose â to ensure that some people have not voted.â Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals opinion

On Oct. 9, a U.S. district judge ruled that the Justice Departmentâs national effort to acquire and share state voter rolls was an illegal abuse of its authority. A Justice Department spokesperson said the department is âreviewing the ruling.â
